name: Khiamniungan Naga (Retired)
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.note: Retired Glottolog bookkeeping node: ISO nky split 2008 into kix/pzn/jmn (CR 2007-252); no references attach to it

sources.citation: van Dam, Kellen Parker & Keen Thaam. 2026. Wolam Ngio, a Khiamniungic variety of Nagaland. In: Lesser Known Languages of Northeast India, pp. 151-169. Guwahati. ISBN 978-81-99105-2-4. (Zenodo doi:10.5281/zenodo.18650479)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Section 3 Phonology (pp. 159-164): onsets, codas, vowels, five phonemic tones (pitch primary, duration secondary), minimal tone sandhi. Stress is only mentioned incidentally: vowels 'centralise to some degree' in unstressed positions, and a schwa-like suffix is 'one of only a very small number of morphemes which never occur in stressed position' (p. 160). No statement of where word stress falls.

sources.citation: van Dam, Kellen Parker. 2026 (pre-publication copy dated 2024). Patkaian (Northern Naga). In: The Oxford Guide to the Tibeto-Burman Languages. OUP. (Zenodo doi:10.5281/zenodo.22253033)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Sec. 3.1 Phonology / 3.1.1 Tone & Phonation: family-wide sesquisyllabic CəCV[CN] syllable structure, 3-5 lexical tones; Khiamniungan and Gongvangpounyiu tonogenesis independent of the north; Khiamniungan lacks a checked-tone category. Nothing on word stress.

sources.note: Morphology paper on the standard Thang dialect; only a passing mention of a 'tonal effect' of the imperative prefix a-. Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: van Dam, Kellen Parker. 2018. The tone system of Tangsa-Nocte and related northern Naga varieties. PhD thesis, La Trobe University. doi:10.26181/21858474

sources.citation: Coupe, Alexander R. 2014. Strategies for analyzing tone languages. Language Documentation & Conservation 8: 462-489. http://hdl.handle.net/10125/24614
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Preliminary tonal analysis of the Thang dialect of Khiamniungan (kix): six pitches initially recognised [55 51 33 31 21 35], [31]/[21] later collapsed, i.e. five tones incl. a rising tone (pp. 473-474); notes Weidert 1987 analysed six tones. Discusses list intonation on disyllables (khə³¹thaʔ³³ 'above'). No statement about word stress.
